summary: Updates RFC 2460 to clarify how intermediate IPv6 nodes should handle extension headers, including ones defined in the future. It also specifies how extension headers are registered by IANA, with a minor update to RFC 2780.

eli5.summary: Packages may have extra labels. This tells the mail carriers on the way how to treat labels they have not seen.

subtitle: Tells routers and firewalls not to drop IPv6 packets just because they carry extension headers the device does not recognise.

tldr.problem: Firewalls and other middleboxes often drop IPv6 packets with extension headers they do not recognise, which blocks newly standardised headers from being deployed.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that all forwarding nodes should pass packets regardless of extension headers, that any discard of a standard header must be a configurable policy, and that IANA keeps a registry of extension header types.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2460 and RFC 2780, but it does not fix the underlying design of extension headers, so new headers may still fail on some paths.

today: RFC 7045 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2460 and RFC 2780. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 7045 itself.

sections.title: The Problem with IPv6 Extension Headers
sections.content:
In IPv6, an extension header is any header that follows the initial 40 bytes of the packet and precedes the upper-layer header. RFC 2460 said extension headers are not examined or processed by any node along the path until the packet reaches the node named in the Destination Address field, with the exception of the Hop-by-Hop Options header. Forwarding nodes were meant to be transparent to them, so new headers could be introduced gradually.

In practice that is not what happens. Routers and middleboxes such as firewalls, load balancers and packet classifiers sometimes inspect the whole packet, which means walking the chain of extension headers to find the transport header. Because not all extension headers use a uniform TLV format, this is clumsy, and it may be too slow for line-speed processing.

Some firewalls treat an unrecognised extension header as suspect and drop the packet. The RFC states that several widely used firewalls do not recognise some or all headers standardised after RFC 2460, and some do not handle even the fragment header.
sections.eli5: The rule was that only the final receiver reads the extra labels. But some helpers along the way peek at them anyway, and some throw away any package with a label they have never seen.

sections.title: A Catch-22 for New Headers
sections.content:
Extension headers are numbered out of the existing IP Protocol Number space, so there is no collected list of them. An implementor who consults only RFC 2460 will miss every header defined later.

This creates what the RFC calls a Catch-22 for any newly standardised extension header, except for local use. It cannot be widely deployed because existing middleboxes will drop it on many paths. Yet most middleboxes will not be updated to let it pass until it has been proved safe and useful on the open Internet, which cannot happen until they are updated.

The uniform TLV format in RFC 6564 helps, but only for future extensions. The RFC also says it does not intend to solve the fundamental architectural problem, and that fundamental changes to the extension header architecture are out of scope.
sections.eli5: It is a chicken-and-egg problem. Nobody updates the gatekeepers until a new label proves useful, and the label cannot prove useful while the gatekeepers keep throwing it away.

sections.title: What Forwarding Nodes Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC uses forwarding node for any router, firewall, load balancer, prefix translator or other middlebox that forwards IPv6 packets. It defines standard extension headers as those specified by IETF Standards Actions, experimental ones as those in Experimental RFCs plus values 253 and 254, and defined as both together.

  • A forwarding node SHOULD forward a packet regardless of extension headers, as RFC 2460 requires.
  • If a node is designed to examine extension headers, for firewalling for example, it MUST recognise and deal appropriately with all standard types and SHOULD do so for experimental types.
  • Intermediate nodes SHOULD NOT discard packets just because of an unrecognised header. Destination hosts are still required by RFC 2460 to discard such packets.
  • Discarding a packet with a standard header MUST be the result of a configurable policy, individually configurable per header type, and the default SHOULD allow all standard headers.
  • Experimental headers SHOULD be treated the same way, but the default MAY drop them.
  • Nodes MUST be configurable to allow unrecognised extension headers, though the default MAY drop such packets.

Routing Header Types 0 and 1 are deprecated, but that does not mean the Routing Header can always be dropped. Undeprecated types such as Type 2, Type 3 and the experimental Types 253 and 254 SHOULD be forwarded by default.
sections.eli5: Helpers along the way should pass packages along even with labels they do not know. They may only throw one away if someone deliberately set a rule saying so.

sections.title: Hop-by-Hop Options
sections.content:
The Hop-by-Hop Options header SHOULD be processed by intermediate forwarding nodes as described in RFC 2460. The RFC admits this is often unrealistic: high-performance routers are expected either to ignore it or to put packets containing it on a slow processing path.

Designers planning to use a hop-by-hop option therefore need to be aware of that likely behaviour. The RFC also reminds readers that, under RFC 2460, the Hop-by-Hop Options header must come first if present.
sections.eli5: One special label asks every helper along the way to read it. Fast helpers usually skip it or set the package aside for later, so do not count on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Forwarding nodes that act as firewalls MUST follow the requirements above, so packets with standard extension headers are discarded only by an intentionally configured policy. The changes do not stop a firewall from filtering unwanted or suspect headers, but they do require it to be able to permit any or all of them.

Types 253 and 254 can be used either for experimental extension headers or for experimental payload types, and an IPv6 header has no length field, so there is no generic algorithm for a firewall to tell which it is. That should be considered when choosing the default action for those values.

Newly defined headers will exercise new code paths in a host that recognises them, so caution may be needed. The RFC expects deployment to be slow and to depend on operational experience, and until then a new extension will fail in some parts of the Internet.
sections.eli5: Gatekeepers can still block labels on purpose. They just have to be able to let any label through if told to. Brand-new labels will take a long time to be accepted everywhere.

sections.title: The IANA Registry of Extension Headers
sections.content:
IANA added a column called IPv6 Extension Header to the Assigned Internet Protocol Numbers registry, marking values that are also extension header types. It closed the existing empty Next Header Types registry to new entries and redirected users to a new IPv6 Extension Header Types registry. References to the IPv6 Next Header field in RFC 2780 are to be read as also applying to the IPv6 Extension Header field, which is the minor update to RFC 2780.

The initial list has these values: 0 Hop-by-Hop Option, 43 Routing Header, 44 Fragment Header, 50 Encapsulating Security Payload, 51 Authentication Header, 60 Destination Options, 135 Mobility Header, 139 Host Identity Protocol (experimental use), 140 Shim6 Protocol, and 253 and 254 for experimentation and testing. Type 59, No Next Header, is excluded because it is not an extension header as such.
sections.eli5: The RFC asks for one official list of every extra label, so builders no longer have to hunt through old documents to learn which ones exist.
